Good news and bad news on this. Let me lay out what I found.

**Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD) layer is power-only, confirmed.** I checked its actual attributes: `NAICS_DESC = "ELECTRIC BULK POWER TRANSMISSION AND CONTROL"`, a `VOLTAGE` field, owners like "ALABAMA POWER CO". Zero relation to data networks — that layer stays as-is.

**A true "all US data-carrying fiber networks" layer doesn't exist as a downloadable dataset — for the same reason Lumen only gives you an interactive map, not a download.** Carriers treat exact fiber routes as proprietary/security-sensitive info, and this isn't unique to Lumen:
- HIFLD (the government's infrastructure-data clearinghouse, same source as your power-lines layer) has never published a route-level nationwide fiber layer — it's excluded for the same critical-infrastructure-sensitivity reasons.
- The one open global fiber-mapping effort I found (OFDS/OpenFiberMap) has zero US coverage — 24 countries, US isn't one of them.
- OpenStreetMap's fiber tags exist but are too sparse in the US to be usable (not enough contributors map buried conduit).
- Your project already has `Internet2 Physical Routes` — that's real fiber route data, but it's one network (a research/education backbone), same "single company" problem as Lumen.

So there's no single clean source. Here are the realistic options, each a different tradeoff:

questions.question: Given there's no single authoritative multi-carrier fiber route dataset, which approach should the new data-network layer use?

options.label: FCC fiber availability (Recommended)
options.description: FCC Broadband Data Collection: real government data reported by every ISP nationwide, shows where fiber-based data service is available. Not exact conduit routes, but genuinely multi-carrier and comprehensive (all companies, not just one).

options.label: Likely fiber-corridor proxy
options.description: Add Interstate highways + active rail lines as a labeled 'likely fiber corridor' layer, since long-haul carriers overwhelmingly bury conduit along these rights-of-way. Route-shaped lines nationwide, but it's an inference, not verified placement — would be clearly labeled as such.

options.label: Verified networks only
options.description: Stick to networks with confirmed public route data: keep Internet2, and add other real ones I can find (e.g. ESnet, the Dept. of Energy's science network). Smaller and incomplete, but everything shown is 100% real, not inferred.

options.label: State broadband office data
options.description: Many states publish 'existing fiber infrastructure' GIS layers (compiled from ISPs for federal BEAD grant mapping) — most accurate option, but state-by-state, slower to assemble, and only covers states that publish it.

1	# US Fiber & Data Infrastructure Map — Data Sources & Methodology Log
2	
3	Project file: `100_gqis_source.qgz`
4	Log created: 2026-09-21
5	
6	This log records where every layer in the project came from, why it was built the way
7	it was, and what limitations to keep in mind when citing this map in the thesis.
8	
9	## Current layers
10	
11	### Submarine Cables (TeleGeography, all)
12	- **Submarine Cables** (729 features) — merged from 708 separate single-cable layers
13	  that were originally split across individual tables in `telegeography_cables_by_name.gpkg`
14	  (each cable was its own layer, tanking QGIS performance). Merged via
15	  `native:mergevectorlayers` into `telegeography_cables_merged.gpkg`, verified feature
16	  count matched (729 in, 729 out) before the original 708-table file was deleted.
17	  Styled with a data-defined stroke color pulled from each feature's own `color`
18	  attribute (the dataset's built-in per-cable color scheme).
19	  - **Backups made before the merge:** `100_gqis_source_backup_20260921_143340.qgz`,
20	    `telegeography_cables_by_name_backup_20260921_143340.gpkg`
21	
22	### US Internal Fiber (Internet2 + PeeringDB)
23	- **Internet2 Physical Routes** (91 features) — real, traced physical fiber/leased
24	  routes of Internet2's US research & education backbone. Source: Internet2's own
25	  published network map (`internet2.edu/infrastructure/i2-network-map`), which is
26	  built with `qgis2web` and exposes its underlying GeoJSON directly
27	  (`Network_3.js`). Categorized by `key`: `fiber` (owned dark fiber, long-haul),
28	  `leased` (short metro-local circuits), `infrastructure` (one segment,
29	  Sunnyvale↔LA — likely shared partner-network capacity, exact meaning not
30	  documented by Internet2).
31	- **Internet2 Sites** (195 features) — Optical Sites, Packet Sites, NAREX
32	  Exchanges, Regional Exchanges, and Cloud Onramps, also from Internet2's
33	  published map data.
34	- **Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD)** (93,996 features) — real electric power
35	  transmission line geometry (69kV–765kV), clipped to CONUS. Source: HIFLD Next
36	  (`hifld.publicenvirodata.org`), the community-preserved successor to DHS's
37	  HIFLD Open portal (shut down August 2025). Styled by voltage class. Note: this
38	  is electric grid infrastructure, not a data/cable network — kept in the project
39	  as context (matches the style of NREL's US data infrastructure map), removed
40	  and restored once at the user's request.
41	- **Removed from this group:** *Internet2 NAREX Links* (schematic straight-line
42	  connections representing peering relationships with partner research networks,
43	  not real traced fiber paths — removed since it isn't an actual physical cable
44	  route). *Data Centers & Carrier Facilities (PeeringDB)* and *Equinix Data
45	  Centers* and *Notable Data Centers (Wikidata)* — superseded by the FracTracker-based
46	  Data Centers layer, see below.
47	
48	### Data Centers (FracTracker, Operating)
49	- **Data Centers (Operating)** (447 features) — sourced entirely from the user's
50	  own spreadsheet, `Copy of Data_Centers_Database.xlsx`, compiled by **FracTracker
51	  Alliance** (an environmental-advocacy nonprofit; data collected via media
52	  monitoring, permits, FOIA requests, and crowdsourcing —
53	  see `fractracker.org/data-centers`). Filtered to rows where `status = Operating`
54	  **and** at least one `info_source` citation is populated (447 of 1,684 total
55	  rows in the spreadsheet; the rest are Proposed/Permitted/Cancelled/Suspended or
56	  uncited). Single uniform icon per the user's request (no source-based styling).
57	  - **Attribution requirement:** FracTracker's terms of service require citation
58	    wherever this data is used publicly: *"Data provided by FracTracker Alliance,
59	    accessed via https://www.fractracker.org/data-centers/"* — this is baked into
60	    the layer's metadata abstract, but **must also be included in any thesis
61	    figure or published map** using this layer.
62	  - Earlier iterations of this layer merged in PeeringDB (664), Equinix official
63	    addresses (73, scraped from equinix.com facility pages), and Wikidata (15
64	    notable facilities). This was later simplified to FracTracker-only per the
65	    user's request for one unified icon and one source.
66	
67	### US Cable Landing Stations (19 features) — unchanged from original project.
68	
69	## What was investigated but NOT used (and why)
70	
71	A full nationwide dataset of *actual commercial long-haul fiber routes* does not
72	exist in any accessible open form. Investigated and ruled out:
73	- **HIFLD's historical "Long Haul Fiber" layer** — no longer exists anywhere in
74	  the HIFLD Next archive (confirmed by searching the full 400+ layer catalog).
75	- **InterTubes** (Durairajan et al., UW-Madison, SIGCOMM 2015) — the most
76	  credible academic long-haul fiber map exists, but is access-gated via IMPACT
77	  Cybertrust (DHS-affiliated), requiring an account and approved data request.
78	- **Internet Atlas** (same UW-Madison team) — project domain (`internetatlas.org`)
79	  no longer resolves; effectively dead.
80	- **NREL's own "US Data Infrastructure" map** — confirmed to be a flat image
81	  only; NREL's own write-up states fiber routes are "estimated" and the map
82	  "cannot be made available as an interactive web map due to the sensitive and
83	  proprietary nature of the data."
84	- **Carrier-published maps** (Lumen, Zayo, etc.) — schematic marketing diagrams
85	  (straight city-to-city lines), not real geometry; several are gated behind
86	  lead-generation forms.
87	- **Equinix's own interactive map data** — deliberately obfuscated/encoded
88	  client-side against bulk extraction; not attempted to reverse-engineer.
89	- **SEC 10-K filings** (Digital Realty) — Item 2/Schedule III property
90	  disclosures are legally required but only report **metro-level aggregates**
91	  ("Northern Virginia: 16 buildings"), not individual addresses.
92	- **OpenStreetMap Overpass API** — public instances were unreachable/overloaded
93	  for the entire session; not pursued further given US fiber-tagging coverage in
94	  OSM is sparse anyway.
95	
96	## Key methodology notes for the thesis write-up
97	
98	1. Any claim that this map shows "the fiber network" should be scoped precisely:
99	   it shows Internet2's real backbone + submarine cable landings + data center
100	   locations, **not** the commercial carrier long-haul backbone, which remains
101	   non-public.
102	2. Data center coverage is real and sourced, but not exhaustive — FracTracker's
103	   collection methodology is advocacy-driven (skews toward large/newsworthy
104	   facilities); smaller low-profile colocation buildings may be under-represented.
105	3. All removed layers still exist in `us_internal_fiber.gpkg` (their GeoPackage
106	   tables were never deleted, only unlinked from the project) — anything can be
107	   re-added if needed later.
108

content.text: This project already has extensive prior research on exactly this problem — a `data_sources_and_methodology_log.md` documents that Lumen-style carrier maps, HIFLD's fiber layer, NREL's map, and academic long-haul datasets were all already investigated and ruled out for the same reasons I was independently finding. Good news: the FCC Broadband Data Collection county layer I just added isn't in that log — it's a genuinely new, legitimate source. I'll make it permanent the way the rest of this project's layers are handled (local GeoPackage, not a live remote dependency) and log it consistently.

### US Cable Landing Stations (19 features) — unchanged from original project.

### Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)
- **Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)** (3,234 features) — county-level
  fixed-broadband availability statistics from the FCC's Broadband Data Collection (BDC),
  pulled via Esri's public "FCC Broadband Data Collection December 2025" Feature Service
  (`services8.arcgis.com/.../FCC_Broadband_Data_Collection_December_2024_View`), which
  republishes FCC BDC data without requiring the paid CostQuest Broadband Serviceable
  Location Fabric. Exported to a local snapshot
  (`fcc_bdc_fiber_availability_by_county.gpkg`) rather than kept as a live service, for
  reproducibility. Added a computed field, `PctFiberCoverage = ServedBSLsFiber /
  TotalBSLs * 100`, and styled as a 5-class graduated choropleth (Blues ramp), placed
  beneath the point/line layers in draw order so it doesn't obscure them.
  - **What this is / isn't:** NOT traced fiber route geometry — it's every ISP's
    self-reported service availability, aggregated to the county polygon and summed
    across every provider reporting fiber (technology code 50) to the FCC. It answers
    "how much of this county can get fiber-based broadband, from any provider" — the
    multi-carrier counterpart the project was missing (Internet2 above is one network's
    real routes; this is every reporting ISP — Lumen, AT&T, Verizon, etc. included — but
    as availability stats, not physical routes). The source table also carries
    `UniqueProvidersFiber` (count of distinct fiber ISPs per county, kept but not used
    for styling) if that's useful later.
  - This is a different FCC data product (regulatory availability reporting) from the
    route-level "Long Haul Fiber" datasets ruled out below — it wasn't part of that
    earlier investigation.

**Done.** Summary:

- **Power Transmission Lines (HIFLD)** is confirmed electric-power-only — checked its actual attributes (NAICS "ELECTRIC BULK POWER TRANSMISSION AND CONTROL", voltage field, power-company owners). Left untouched, as requested.
- **New layer added:** "Fiber Broadband Availability (FCC BDC, by County)" — 3,234 US counties, choropleth by `PctFiberCoverage`, sitting beneath your existing point/line layers so it doesn't bury them. Sourced from the FCC's Broadband Data Collection (every ISP that reports fiber service to the FCC — AT&T, Verizon, Lumen, etc. all included as availability stats, not just Internet2), exported to a local `.gpkg` snapshot for reproducibility.
- This is genuinely multi-carrier, unlike Internet2 (one network) or Lumen (one company, and not downloadable anyway) — but it's availability-by-county, not traced route geometry, since (per your own methodology log, which I read before doing more redundant digging) actual nationwide multi-carrier fiber *routes* don't exist in any public downloadable form — carriers treat them as proprietary/sensitive, same reason HIFLD, NREL, and the academic InterTubes/Internet Atlas datasets were all already ruled out.
- Logged the addition in [data_sources_and_methodology_log.md](C:\Users\Vy\Desktop\thesis\100_thesis_beginnings\100_qgis_fiber_networks\data_sources_and_methodology_log.md) in the same style as your existing entries, including an explicit "don't conflate this with real routes" caution, and saved the project.

One thing worth flagging: the layer landed in its own new group at the bottom of the tree; I couldn't reorder it relative to the *other* groups (QGIS's reorder tool only works within one group), so if you want it interleaved differently, that'd need manual drag-and-drop in QGIS.
